conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, Mr. ___. I'm Dr. ___, one of the hospital doctors. You're here because of severe abdominal pain and diarrhea. Can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, doctor. For the last few days, I’ve been going to the bathroom every 20 to 30 minutes—up to 40 times a day. It’s watery, not bloody, but the pain in my lower left belly is terrible.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That sounds very uncomfortable. You mentioned this feels similar to past Crohn’s flares?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. It’s just like before—same kind of cramping, same urgency. But this time it came on fast.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve had a subtotal colectomy, so you don’t have a colon anymore, but the inflammation can still happen in your small intestine and rectum.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Right. And I’ve been on prednisone at home—30 mg daily, up from 15 mg. But it’s not helping enough.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve reviewed your labs. Your white count is a bit high, and your bicarbonate is low—14—which suggests metabolic acidosis, possibly from dehydration due to the diarrhea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been drinking, but I can’t keep up. I also feel lightheaded sometimes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. We’re going to keep you NPO—nothing by mouth—for now to let your bowel rest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Nothing to eat or drink? Even water?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll give you IV fluids to keep you hydrated. You can’t eat or drink yet, but we’ll reassess tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I trust you. But please, I need something for the pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve given you IV hydromorphone in the ER, and we’ll continue pain control. We also started IV steroids—methylprednisolone—to reduce the inflammation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Steroids again? I’m already on prednisone. Is this safe?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, because this is a flare, we need higher-dose IV steroids to get it under control quickly. We’ll transition back to oral prednisone as you improve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on steroids for years. I lost my left testicle—got hard after long-term use. I worry about side effects.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand your concern. We’re using this short-term to treat the flare. Your gastroenterologist will help you taper slowly to minimize side effects.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that helps. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your pain is a bit better today, I hear. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still painful, but not as intense. I haven’t had the urge to go as often—maybe 10 times since last night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good sign. Your labs this morning show your bicarbonate is improving—up to 20. Your kidney function is also better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the IV fluids are helping?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and the steroids are starting to work. The GI team recommends starting clear liquids today—water, broth, apple juice—see how you tolerate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I have coffee? I usually drink a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. Caffeine can irritate your gut. We’ll keep it caffeine-free and low-residue for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Understood. What about my omeprazole for acid reflux?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve been giving you IV pantoprazole, which is similar. Once you’re on full oral intake, we’ll switch back to your usual omeprazole.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ve had GERD for years. Don’t want that flaring too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did well with clear liquids. We’re advancing you to a low-residue, lactose-free diet—soft foods like mashed potatoes, applesauce, and toast.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That sounds better than nothing. How long until I can eat normally?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It depends on how you respond. If your bowel movements stay controlled, we’ll keep progressing. We also got your stool tests back—no infection found.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not food poisoning or something I caught?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No. No C. diff, no Salmonella, Shigella, or parasites. This looks like a Crohn’s flare, not an infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I was worried about that. So the steroids are doing the job?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’re switching from IV to oral prednisone today—60 mg daily. You’ll need to taper it slowly with your gastroenterologist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: 60 mg? That’s higher than I was on.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but only for a short burst to control the flare. Then you’ll taper down over weeks. Stopping suddenly could cause a rebound.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ll follow up with my GI doctor right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. You’re looking better. Pain down to a 3 out of 10?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, much better. I’ve had only five bowel movements since yesterday morning, and they’re more formed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. Your labs this morning show your hemoglobin dropped a bit—to 12.7—but it’s stable. We’ll keep monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had anemia before. Is it related to Crohn’s?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, chronic inflammation and poor absorption can cause it. You’re still getting B12 shots monthly, which helps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I get those at my GI clinic. Should I keep doing that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, definitely. We’ll send you home with a prescription to continue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—we’re discharging you today. You’re doing well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What meds am I going home with?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll take prednisone 60 mg daily—six 5 mg tablets—and talk to your GI doctor about tapering. Also, omeprazole once daily, loperamide as needed for diarrhea, and your B12 and calcium.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And pain medicine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, oxycodone-acetaminophen for breakthrough pain, but only as needed. Don’t overuse it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll be careful. Any restrictions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Stick to low-residue, lactose-free, caffeine-free foods for now. Gradually reintroduce others as tolerated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: See your gastroenterologist within a week to discuss the steroid taper and long-term management.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you, doctor. I feel much better than when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’re glad we could help. Take care, and call if symptoms return.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—my skin rash. It’s healing, but still itchy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve prescribed bacitracin ointment—apply it twice daily. It should continue improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. I’ll use it as directed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re all set. The nurse will bring your discharge papers and prescriptions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Appreciate everything. Have a good day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You too. Get some rest and take it easy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care, Mr. ___.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: You too, doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will be in shortly to assist with discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’m ready.
